subtopic: REPORTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ANTI-SABOTAGE ORGANIZATION IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning the Canadian press carried a rather curious news item, about which I should like to ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). Apparently this item emanates from the attorney general of Ontario. The article reads in part:
Establishment in Ontario of a powerful, mobile anti-sabotage organization, to be built from the provincial and municipal police, cooperating with the royal Canadian mounted, and equipped for immediate operation in the event of war or some other dire emergency is now well under way.

Questions
The gentleman who is said to be in charge of this organization is "reporting not only to his immediate superior, Attorney General Conant, but indirectly to a secret committee which has been formed at Ottawa under the Department of National Defence." I should like to ask three questions: (a) Is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police under the direction of the Department of National Defence?
(b)	What is this secret committee which is under the Department of National Defence?
(c)	Under what authority is this powerful, mobile anti-sabotage organization operating?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED ESTABLISHMENT OF ANTI-SABOTAGE ORGANIZATION IN ONTARIO
speechtext: Like my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), I am afraid my memory is not good enough to enable me to remember all the points contained in my hon. friend's query. All I can say is that the mounted police are still under the control of the Minister of Justice. As far as the rest of his question is concerned, the only thing I can make public is that there is the fullest cooperation, and I am glad of it, between the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the provincial forces in all the provinces of Canada, to maintain order in any case of emergency. All precautions are and will be taken for that purpose. I hope it will never be necessary to use the measures of precaution which have been taken, but I think it is a good thing to take these precautions.

speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman has better luck in that regard than I usually have.

I am trusting to the authority of Mr. Speaker and the good sense of the house. This is the only day that this resolution can be brought up; it is an important matter, and a number of hon. members want to speak on it.
Little time need be spent in demonstrating the need for unemployment insurance. Nearly all the important countries of Europe have such a scheme. Britain has had it since 1911. If that is so, why not get together and pass it now and make it unanimous? I know.that we shall immediately be confronted with the bugbear of provincial autonomy. Well, in my humble opinion there is a good deal too much attention paid to the claims of the provinces to be self-governing bodies. I think it largely arises from an exaggerated idea of their own importance held by certain local politicians, and was never intended by the British North America Act.
Only two ways appear to present themselves, ordinarily speaking, of meeting the situation. One is to try to persuade the three provinces to join with the rest of us in a petition to the

In view of the Quebec speech from the throne the other day, and other utterances, that way out is apparently beyond hope; at least there is very little to be hoped for. But I submit that there is a third way that might present a reasonable solution of the matter without asking the provinces to do something that we know they will not do, and without trying to force them to do something which we know we cannot make them do.
In the United States the same relation obtains between the federal government and the states as obtains in Canada between the dominion government and the provinces. In both cases the federal authority are unable to pass constitutional unemployment insurance legislation and they are equally unable to force the states or the provinces, as the case may be, to do so either. I suggest that we follow the clever manner in which the Washington government got around the difficulty and, by introducing perfectly legal legislation, brought about, without compulsion, state legislation on unemployment insurance. I referred to this matter in 1934. It was brought up in Washington at that time by a man named Wagner as a private member, but since then the government has taken it up. In January, 1935, the government of the United States introduced what is known as the Social Security Act, a copy of which can be obtained in our library. That act covered many phases of social security such as old age, maternity cases, children, unemployment insurance and so on. Each was dealt with in a separate chapter, but I propose to deal only with the unemployment insurance phase.
There were three objections fatal to the federal legislation, and equally so as regards the dominion. One was that the federal authority could not pass unemployment insurance; the second was that they could not compel the states to do so; and the third, which was the most important one, was that if two or three states did pass such legislation, the cost, which would undoubtedly come out of the payroll in whole or part, would have to be added to the cost of the manufactured article, and those states that followed that course would be handicapped in

The Social Security Act met all these difficulties. It did not pass unemployment insurance by itself; it did not compel the states to do anything; but it did protect those states that would pass such legislation, and

it produced unemployment insurance. All it did was to produce a desire on the part of the states to pass such legislation, but there was no compulsion, as we shall see. The preamble of the act declared that it was proposed to legislate for the general welfare by doing such and so, and to help the administration-only the administration-of their unemployment compensation laws of the various states. The word "compensation" was used instead of insurance. Nothing is said about unemployment insurance, but merely that they are willing to help to pay the administration costs of unemployment insurance where it exists. Of course, it is obvious that you could not pay the administration costs in those places where they did not have an act of that kind.
Section 303 of the act lays down a few simple conditions that hardly require anything at all except that the state shall have such a scheme, and shall pay money to unemployed people. That is really all. Subsection 4 of section 303 provides that all funds collected by the state under any state scheme shall be paid into a central fund held by the federal authorities, and each state can take out of the fund whenever it likes everything it has put into it, and no more, provided the money is used for the payment of unemployment insurance. But they do not pay for the administration cost because the federal authorities pay that. In other words, the state starts a system of insurance, practically in any form it likes, and collects the cost in the shape of taxes, then pays them into the central fund and draws it all out to pay insurance but not the management, the federal authority paying all costs of administration. The states know, therefore, that if they start such a scheme the federal authorities will pay the costs of administration but there is no compulsion and therefore no interference with jurisdiction.
The matter has been tested and found absolutely legal. It might be held that the cost of administration, although very considerable, did not represent a sufficient inducement to the states to introduce unemployment insurance. Well, there is another section of the act to which I will refer. It is not compulsory. They so arrange it that the legislatures of the states feel impelled, not compelled, to adopt such legislation. Section 901 of the 
act imposed an excise tax-that is the word used-on all employers of labour throughout the whole of the United States, employing more than eight persons. It began with one per cent, but it is now three per cent of the payroll. That is paid over to the federal authorities. It is not earmarked in any way to be used for any particular purpose but is simply paid into the national revenue just as if we paid similar sums into the consolidated revenue fund. It is an absolutely legal excise tax imposed for a national purpose, but that purpose is nowhere indicated; unemployment insurance is not mentioned from beginning to end.
But-and here is the crux of the whole situation-section 902 provides that anyone paying this sum, which of course he has to pay, can deduct ninety per cent of it if a similar sum has been paid under the terms of a state unemployment insurance scheme. Suppose a company had a payroll of $50,000 a year. That company would have to pay SI,500 to the federal authorities, and they would have to pay that amount in any event, and they would get no obvious return for it. But if there was a local state scheme, any sum which the company paid towards that state scheme could be deducted from the contribution paid to the federal authorities. The situation then is this: Business men, who are the biggest taxpayers as a rule, say to themselves, to their friends, and to the legislators, "We have to pay three per cent on our payroll of $50,000, and we shall never see it again. But if we had a state unemployment insurance scheme the money would be all spent in the state. It would save our relief bills, make labour more satisfied and reduce the labour turnover. The alternatives are to pay it all to Washington or to have it spent within the state." And so they bring pressure to bear on their legislators to get a state law passed. I maintain that the same thing would happen in the provinces of Canada.
The outstanding objection I have mentioned, that two or three states who did adopt the scheme would be handicapped in the sale of their products, inasmuch as they would have to pay this money directly or indirectly, whereas other states would not, has been met and done away with. For the man has to pay three per cent in any case, and if he has a state unemployment insurance scheme to contribute to the money is devoted to that purpose. In any event he is bound to pay $1,500, in the case I have given by way of illustration, and if it does not go to support a state scheme it all goes to Washington. The only choice he has is this: Will he pay it all to Washington and get no immediate, visible benefit from it, or will he pay it into the

The federal authorities in Washington give a wide latitude to the states in their acts. They are practically free to draw up any kind of act they like provided it is of that character. They can raise money as they like; it need not be three per cent on their payroll. They can make employees contribute if they think fit, or they can pay part out of general taxation. It is practically left to every state to do exactly as it likes. And it is noteworthy that while this bill was introduced by the Democrats in Washington it was supported by the Republicans and passed unanimously.
We have before us, then, this entirely voluntary system, newly introduced and until then untried. Let us look at the results. That bill was passed finally in August, 1935. By the middle of 1937 every state and territory in the United States of America had passed an unemployment insurance law. They did not have to, there was no compulsion; and it is noteworthy, almost miraculous, that every last one passed such a law within that period. Some 21,000,000 people were covered. That is an achievement to be proud of, bringing the benefits of unemployment insurance to 21,000,000 people. More than that, all but two of those states are now paying the unemployment insurance benefit, although there was generally a two year interval; but now they are all paying except two states, I think, Illinois and Montana, which will be paying by July of this year. While each state had an absolutely free hand it is remarkable to see how comparatively similar was the legislation they passed. The cost has been calculated at an average of about 2-7 per cent of the payroll; in five or six states it runs to a little more, and in six states the employees have to contribute as well. That is entirely optional. None of the states pay anything towards it from general taxation; either the employer pays or the employer and employee jointly. In every case the administration costs are paid by the federal authorities.
This year in the speech from the throne the government were able to say no more than that they hoped to get further cooperation from the provinces in connection with such a scheme, and that they were still of the opinion-and so on. should have to wait for the Rowell commission to report; then we have the visit of their majesties, and there might be an election. The system I have presented is not some ephemeral scheme thought up by myself; it is one which is in actual effect under conditions very much like ours. We have the object lesson of how it was done and the experience of applying it to 21,000,000 people. Surely among that 21,000,000 we can find conditions similar to our own here. If we adopt this scheme we might be paying benefits inside of two years, with no long dispute with two or more provinces and all the bitterness that interprovincial enmity provokes.
I suggest that delay in this matter is unnecessary and might well be dangerous. People are in a sensitive mood, and if they get the idea that nothing is going to be done for them they will get bitter. If a man quarrels and you can reason with him you can abate his anger, but if he gets in a sullen mood you can do nothing with him. There is nothing more hopeless than a body of people who have arrived at the condition of hopelessness and helplessness, and who believe in nothing and nobody; they are ready to bite at any ridiculous promise, and might by pressure pass legislation which would be disastrous to themselves and equally disastrous to other people.

It will not do away with unemployment, but it will cushion the disaster and injury that unemployment produces to the whole body politic; for it extends beyond the particular wmrking man concerned-it affects us all. Therefore I am convinced that the resolution introduced by the hon. member is one that should receive our immediate attention.
I do not agree with him that every hon. member of this house supports the principle of unemployment insurance. I have talked to a good number and 1 find that we are not all agreed on the principle of unemployment insurance and the advantages which it offers. For this reason I propose to examine, dispassionately, I hope, some of the economic implications of the resolution. I propose to be as realistic as possible in my treatment of the question. I do not propose to assume, as my hon. friends immediately opposite would assume, that the form of economic society under which we operate is one that should be done away with. I prefer to recognize that in Canada there is not much likelihood that this system of free competition will cease to exist, in our immediate time. We have to approach the problem as legislators with this assumption ever in mind.
Under our competitive and acquisitive system unemployment is inevitable; we might as well recognize this. That is exactly what a great economist, and one of the greatest authorities on this subject, meant when he wrote:
So long as the industrial world is split up into separate groups of producers, each group with a life of its own and growing or decaying in ceaseless attrition upon its neighbours, there must be insecurity of employment. It is probable that at least one of the most striking specific factors in the problem, namely, cyclical fluctuation of trade, may be traced ultimately to the same source. Unemployment in other 
words is to some extent at least part of the price of industrial competition, part of the waste without which there could be no competition at all.
So that if we are inevitably to have a constant measure of unemployment in this country we have to find some method whereby those who are engaged in our factories, men and women, will be afforded, in so far as the annual income for their work is concerned. This unemployment inevitably is due in Canada, I suggest, to at least five circumstances-seasonal fluctuations, cyclical depressions, technological developments, the decay and merging of industries, and industrial disputes. I have not the time to analyse each of these, except to say that operations in the automobile industry in my own constituency, the city of Windsor, an industry which at the present time means so much to the economy of Canada, but nevertheless an industry based upon the principle of mass production, in the face of technological developments have resulted in the displacement of human effort by the machine. And to suggest that this substitution is wrong or that we must get away from mass production is not facing the facts.
This civilization of ours is a machine civilization. There is no more chance of getting back to the handicrafts or to barter methods than there is of our having utopia to-morrow. We might as well recognize this. One of- the machines in the automobile industry, a special machine for the manufacture of pressed steel frames, operated by one man, produces six springs per minute, 3,600 in ten hours

an output which by hand methods would require 175 men. This simple illustration indicates the relation of the technological developments which have taken place in industry in respect of what I call the inevitable circumstance of unemployment, under our system of free competition and production.
