I was discussing the question of unemployment reserves as opposed to an insurance scheme. The Wisconsin plan of unemployment reserves seems to be the most successful, but relatively it has been very unsuccessful. That plan shows the weaknesses of an unemployment reserve system as opposed to an unemployment insurance scheme. There are at least two weaknesses in the Wisconsin plan of unemployment reserves. First, it fails to provide for governmental contributions, and, second, it neglects to take advantage of another basic principle of social insurance, namely, the distribution of the burden on all elements of society. I think it is sheer nonsense to argue whether or not unemployment is an incurable risk. That is a metaphysical question which I do not think lawyers or parliamentarians, let alone philosophers, can possibly answer. The real concern of social insurance is security rather thant the upholding of actuarial principles which must govern in private insurance. I am prepared to admit that on a purely actuarial basis a complete system of unemployment insurance in Canada is not possible. That being so, there must be a constant demand on the national exchequer to bolster up a subsidized fund.
Unemployment insurance was the logical evolution of the experience of the trade unions. Many trade unions inaugurated a voluntary plan of insurance. While not altogether successful, while the objective in mind was not reached completely, these voluntary insurance schemes advanced to a point where there were a number of fairly comprehensive systems. The trade union voluntary insurance schemes were based largely upon the principle employed in certain municipal insurance schemes, such as the famous Ghent system, that put into force by the city of Dijon and other cities in France. The limitations of the trade union unemployment insurance schemes were the same as those of the municipal schemes. They did not reach a substantial portion of the working public. They were confined essentially to the members of the trade unions. Because they were operated on a voluntary basis, they took in only a small number of the trade union members. Nevertheless the trade union experience, particularly after the government provided subsidies, has been of great value, in that-and I think this is important-it demonstrated the feasibility and practicability of mutual insurance against unemployment. It demonstrated also that governmental subsidies stimulate this protection; for all voluntary plans expanded greatly after the government began to subsidize them. In the
third place, whatever gain was achieved was due to the factor of compulsion; for it soon became evident that if adequate protection against unemployment was to be extended to the majority of wage earners a national system of compulsory insurance for all workers, with the burden distributed among all groups of society and not on one or two, was the only way out.
This experience of the trade unions, and the experience of other countries where compulsory unemployment insurance is now in vogue, reveal a preference over all other schemes of insurance or unemployment assistance, stabilization fund, or share-the-work movement, in the following particulars.
First, a scheme of contributory unemployment insurance on a nation-wide basis, not for any one province but for the whole nation, would assure the widest possible distribution of the risk. Second, by levying contributions on employers, employees and the state, the burden is equitably distributed. Third, by having such participation in the contributions, as in England, the government can shift a considerable share of the burden to the richer classes through graduated income and inheritance taxes. I suggest that these three principles must ever be at the base of what we adopt in Canada; and while those are the three principles I think the main thing to enunciate in this house is that the scheme must be one not for Ontario, not for Quebec but for every part of the country, for economic reasons which I propose to develop.
Everyone is familiar in a general way with the English experience. Suggestions have been made that great weaknesses have crept in, that great abuse has resulted, and so on. I wish to place on Hansard an important quotation from the final report of the royal commission on unemployment insurance in the United Kingdom, issued in November, 1932:
In industry as a whole there are general changes from activity to depression, exaggerated since the war, which involve the idleness for months at a time of a considerable proportion of fit and efficient workers. In the interests of more economic efficiency, even if no other values were brought into account, it is important to preserve the economic capacity of these workers during their unemployment. A system of unemployment insurance and relief maintains the efficiency of the working population during unemployment and tends to check the accentuation of unemployment in periods of general trade depression.
And note further:
Since 1929 unemployment in this country-
That is to say, the United Kingdom.
-although worse has not increased to the extent and in the degree that it has in the United States and other countries. This difference may in part be due to the mainten-
1112	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Martin
ance of working class spending by unemployment relief, when spending generally was contracting and investment in new enterprises drying up. . . . One of the advantages of a self-supporting insurance scheme is that if properly controlled-
That was what I meant when I referred to an organized system of employment exchange offices.
-it accumulates reserves when spending is active and employment is good, to disburse them automatically at the time when trade is depressed, and spending needs to be stimulated in order to give employment. . . .
The economic facts of the unemployment situation must be considered in relation to the social benefits of unemployment insurance and its extension which have outweighed any economic objections.
This was the conviction of a group of competent men who, at the instance of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, examined the operation of unemployment insurance in that country. This was the result of their examination. The truth is that English statesmen and leaders of business for the time being having dispensed with many of the social implications of the classical economists, and are prepared to look at the situation not in the light of theory as it was known in the days of Adam Smith but in the light of the system under which we are operating, with all its difficulties. They saw to it that a minimum of mass purchasing power would be available to the working groups of England; and as a result of unemployment insurance Great Britain has been returning annually about one and a third billion dollars to the unemployed, the sick, the injured, the aged, the widows and the orphans. This has enhanced the internal purchasing power, on the basis of population, to nearly four billion dollars, and as a result English wage rates have been kept in hand, thus ensuring purchasing power to those who continued to work. I submit that the same can be done for Canada.
I realize the difficulties facing the Minister of Labour in his attempt to deal with this problem. I would suggest to him that if we resort to a scheme it must be on a nationwide basis. Otherwise the following burdens and difficulties would result:	First, workpeople who move constantly from one province to another would present a difficulty when one worker would move from an uninsured to an insured province, or vice versa. Second, it would be unfair that the taxpayers of an uninsured province should contribute equally with the taxpayers of an insured province. Third, the producers of the insured province would be saddled with a substantial item of cost which would not be borne by their competitors in uninsured provinces.
IMr. Martin.]
The answer to all these difficulties, we are told, is a constitutional one. We are told that we all want a system of unemployment insurance in Canada, but that because of the judgments of the judicial committee this is not possible. Well, of course, we have to recognize the findings of the judicial committee, and nothing will be gained by disagreeing with those decisions. At this point, however, I believe I should say that this parliament clearly would have the power, without resorting to the provinces, to bring about an amendment to our constitution in order to clearly and unmistakably endow this parliament with the authority now lacking. I realize that to adopt this method of bringing about the desired end might occasion throughout the country a great deal of dissent and possibly further conflict and lack of harmony. I suggest, just as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has suggested, that we might face the emergency; we might realize the difficulty of implementing this legislation and, on the basis of the old age pension scheme, pass a national act making it optional in the case of the provinces. I venture to suggest that public opinion in all these provinces, including my own, would resist any attempt on the part of provincial politicians to interfere with the national interest. Moreover, our financial arrangements with the provinces could be so dealt with as to make it financially worth while in respect of other contractual obligations for any province to accede readily to the opportunities offered by a national scheme.
We are told that the great difficulty lies in the province of Quebec. Seemingly Ontario has signified its willingness to accept a scheme of unemployment insurance, if we can accept the obiter dicta of some of its politicians. But public opinion in the province of Quebec will not support the premier of that province in his opposition to the scheme, even in the form I have now discussed. I quote from a recent statement of Mr. Charpentier, who was and is president of La Confederation des Travailleurs Catholiques dans la province de Quebec:
However, the Canadian Federation of Catholic Workers would not object to the federal government amending the constitution this very-winter, in order to establish a tripartite system of unemployment insurance in this country without any further delay.
There is the observation of the leader of one of the most powerful labour groups in the province of Quebec. They are not willing that opposition to an amendment of the constitution shall interfere with what I believe, with all its limitations, represents in the light

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. MacNicol.
of past experience the only way within our form of society whereby working people can be given a measure of security during periods of unemployment.
In my own city of Windsor-and I know that the Postmaster General will support my statement-one of the most disheartening things-I say this non-politically and I hope *dispassionately-is that healthy men and women, particularly men working in our automobile factories, receive a wage which in the light of its daily amount seems adequate, but in the light of an annual income is insufficient to maintain properly a home in this country on the standards of living we have set up for ourselves. These men are out of work four and five months in the year. I go into their homes, and often am unable to suggest any satisfactory solution. I am convinced that this problem, particularly in respect to secondary industry in our thickly populated industrial centres, would be relieved by the application of a system of unemployment insurance. The Minister of Labour knows as well as I do, if not much better, the economic and social implications of this problem. I am not trying to pit my humble approach against his. He sees it, I am sure, in its national aspects. But I do say to him, speaking for a constituency where the problem is acute, that public opinion will back up this government and this parliament if it assumes in the way indicated the authority which I think it should assume, and that it will condemn politicians in any part of Canada who seem prepared to place the interests of provincial autonomy ahead of what I regard to be the proper treatment of the most disastrous and dangerous problem which confronts Canada and the world at the present time.

I am happy to rise to second the motion introduced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). It is not the first time such a resolution has been introduced in this house. I believe that during the nine years I have been here it has been proposed several times, and I remember having read before I came here that it was introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps). It has often been debated here; and after many years of debate, in due course an unemployment insurance act was passed. I am not going to speak about it at the moment, but later I shall have something to say with regard to it.
For myself, I have been long associated [DOT]with many thousands of workmen; I know- I should know-their problems; I have been
with them on occasions of joy and at times of sorrow, and I know of no occasion on which I felt more grief for the average worker than I did when he was told that his services were no longer required. From long contact with workmen I am a convinced advocate of contributory unemployment insurance. My conviction arises not only through contact with them but from a very exhaustive inquiry into the subject and from observation of unemployment insurance laws in operation in several Europeon countries, particularly in Great Britain, and a thorough study of the acts which have been referred to as operative in the United States.
In former years, and perhaps at the time the hon. member for Winnipeg North first introduced his unemployment insurance resolution. it was necessary to put up an argument for the principle of the measure. This is no longer necessary. As someone said earlier in the debate, the principle is now recognized everywhere. I believe that all reasonable, thinking men are in favour of unemployment insurance. To read the debates which took place in the British House of Commons in 1911 and immediately prior to the adoption in Great Britain of the first unemployment insurance act in the world, would be an interesting occupation for any hon. member who has not done so. To-day everyone who thinks is in favour of unemployment insurance.
Contributory.

What attracts me most to it is the tragedy of the situation here in Canada. In 1935, after as exhaustive an inquiry into the subject as any government has made, the Bennett government enacted unemployment insurance. I supported it as vigorously as I could. I am sorry that it was not placed in operation. I am convinced that had the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett been returned to power in 1935 it would have been put in operation without any reference to the privy council. It might have been contested later on in the courts, but it would then have been operating for at least some time, during which the people of Canada, and particularly the working man-and it is of his interests I am thinking-would have become interested in and familiar with the operation of unemployment insurance.
It was contributory unemployment insurance, was it not?

Absolutely. That is what I am in favour of. I have not heard any other form of insurance debated in this chamber. I did not hear the beginning of
1114	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. MacNicol.
the speech of the hon. member who introduced the motion, but I am satisfied that any scheme he would advocate would be contributory.
It so states in the- resolution.

In reference to the act passed by the preceding government, and in view of the unemployment which again grew to large proportions in the early months of 1938, I wish to read from an editorial in the Toronto Telegram of January 24, which describes the situation as fittingly and truly as it has ever been depicted:
It was a grave misfortune for Canada that the unemployment insurance act passed by parliament in 1935 should have fallen a victim, first, to political jealousy, and later to an adverse court decision upon its constitutionality, because it is in times of increasing industrial activity and employment such as occurred in the last two years-
That is in 1936 and 1937.
-that a strong fund must be collected to meet the calls which arise when depressions strike and workmen lose their jobs.
That editorial tells the true picture. The reason that an unemployment insurance act is not in operation in this country to-day is, I am convinced, political jealousy. The result is that we are back to-day to where we were around 1928 or 1929 when the hon. member for Winnipeg North introduced his first unemployment insurance resolution.
Let me give a brief history of the origin of unemployment insurance. There is nothing new about it, because for decades prior to 1911, in fact in the early part of the nineteenth century, the great labour organizations first began to provide for what was known at that time as unemployment benefits, and from that day they gradually improved upon the principle of providing unemployment benefits. At the same time many great manufacturing concerns began to take up the question, and eventually they themselves adopted a system of out-of-work or unemployment benefits. I have read the story of the great F. I. A. T., works in Italy, the Sandvick steel works in Sweden, the Zeiss works in Germany and the Phillips works in Holland. All these companies had, for years prior to the operation of unemployment insurance proper, their own out-of-work benefit plans that worked satisfactorily. But in 1911 the British government got right down to business and in enacting an unemployment insurance law they had all the experience of the great labour organizations, the large business concerns and the out-of-work benefit societies that had been operating prior to that time. The quantity of data and material that had been accumulated in

those previous years was of great assistance to the British government in enacting the first unemployment insurance scheme adopted by any government.
I am going to touch upon the British unemployment insurance act later on, but I might say at this stage that a number of other nations followed in the wake of what the British government had done. The British government are usually first in all these matters, and in 1911 they passed their act. Austria passed theirs in 1920, Queensland, Australia, in 1922, and Russia in 1922, although I do not believe it is operating now. Italy passed an act in 1923, Poland in 1924, seventeen of the twenty-seven or twenty-eight cantons of Switzerland in 1924, Bulgaria in 1925, and Germany in 1927. All these acts were contributory and compulsory. A number of other nations adopted non-compulsory acts, but as that is not in the line of my argument I will not take up time enumerating the nations that passed such acts.
There are two different governmental situations to consider in the adoption of an unemployment insurance act. First of all there is the state like Great Britain in which there is only one government for the entire country. That applies also to France, Belgium and a number of other European states. Then there is the federal state, illustrated by Germany, Switzerland, Canada and the United States. It is quite obvious that states with single governments, such as Great Britain, can approach a subject of this kind more quickly and effectively than a federal government can, and it is very largely for that reason, I suppose, that Switzerland and Germany, that adopted unemployment insurance, though perhaps not to the same extent as Great Britain, were later than Great Britain in passing legislation. The United States, where the situation is pretty much as it is in Canada, the individual states being largely sovereign, as the provinces are in this dominion, was still later in adopting an unemployment insurance act; and Canada has not yet passed a measure other than the one which w.as thrown out by the privy council.
I have made a thorough investigation into the operations of the unemployment insurance act in the old land. In London there are forty unemployment offices. There are two main unemployment offices, one in what is known as "the city" and the other at Penton-ville in the northeast end of the city. It was to the latter, I believe, that I went when I was last in London. I wish to describe what I saw there. In the old land the employment office and the unemployment office are operated from the same centre, and it should be the

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. MacNicol.
same in this country. I must first of all remark on the courtesy and sympathy shown by the officials in the various unemployment insurance offices, in which I spent a considerable length of time. I cannot say that I received the same service or was shown the-same sympathy in the unemployment offices I visited in Canada. On more than one occasion I telephoned to an unemployment office and the conversation at the other end was more or less discourteous until I told who I was, and then, to my surprise, the voice became more or less courteous. I should like, however, to compliment the officials in the old country on their courtesy and on the manner in which they treated the men. They addressed them as Jack, or Tom, or Fred, and when I asked how they knew these men, the answer was that over the period of years they have been operating since 1911, naturally many men have visited the various unemployment offices a number of times.
When an unemployed worker enters an office in London he first hands in his card on which are a number of stamps. Perhaps the hon. member for Comox-Alberni described it. Every worker has a card with his name on it and a certain number of stamps are necessary for him to obtain unemployment insurance, and are pasted on that card. He hands his card in and then directs his attention to three boards on the office walls, one after the other. To these offices comes information by teletype from every one of the forty offices and the main offices. That report comes in every fifteen minutes and it indicates any positions that are filled or vacancies that occur. Almost as soon as the report is teletyped it is taken off the machine and placed on a board and the workers quickly gather round that board to find out what opportunities are offering. As promptly thereafter as possible the officials list all these positions on a larger board, and finally they have them typewritten and placed where the workers can see them. If a position becomes vacant they write out a card and give it to the worker. If he obtains employment it is reported at once and his record is so noted and the position that had been tabulated as vacant is also erased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my friend will permit, that system recognizes the inseparable nature of the two things, unemployment insurance and the means of finding employment.
Yes, I explained at the beginning that I was strongly in favour of the system that combines the two.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same authority must govern both in order that it may work.

Yes, the one office takes care of both, and I found it working very satisfactorily. The fact is that in 1936, the year previous to my last visit to the old country, the officials told me in London they had placed men in one million jobs, odd jobs of one kind and another, but some of them permanent. In fact the day I was in the Pentonville office a teletype came in asking for eight squads of boilermakers. I asked what they meant by eight squads, and was told that four men made a squad. There was the boilermaker himself, the man who held the rivet up, the boy who tossed the rivet, and I suppose tthe riveter made the fourth. So that thirty-two men were called for in that request. I was tremendously thrilled with the way in which the whole unemployment situation is taken care of.
It is interesting also to see the men coming in to obtain their insurance. The waiting period in Great Britain has now been reduced to three days; formerly it was six. The men receive their pay during four hours a day. They are dealt with expeditiously; an effort is made not to keep them waiting but to send them on as happily as they can. They report on three days-Monday, Wednesday and Friday, in order also to look over the boards and try to obtain a position.
I am not saying that it is possible at the moment to adopt an unemployment insurance scheme in Canada. The government would have to look into that very carefully; it may or may not be possible. The conditions of the country are so serious at the moment that at least a considerable waiting period would probably have to intervene in order to accumulate the necessary fund.
Something was said by a previous speaker in reference to the financial position of the unemployment insurance fund in the old country. I studied that very carefully with the labour office-they gave me all the available information-and it appeared to me that it was in a most satisfactory position and most successful. This is largely due to the fact that never before have there been so many mechanics employed as there are at present in the old land. In 1936 in England the employer contributed 20 cents a week for each employee, the employee 20 cents a week and the government 20 cents a week, and the receipts from those contributions in 1936 amounted to $322,860,000. Adding to that an amount of $995,000 in interest on the rest that they have already laid up makes total receipts of $323,855,000. Out of that they paid in unemployment benefits $220,027,000. The cost of administration was $20,250,000, and other expenses-I suppose printing, etc.,
1116	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. MacNicol.
and perhaps inspectors-$1,467,000; total expenses $266,744,000, including a return of $25,000,000 to the fund which formerly was known as the dole to pay off the debt that accumulated following the war when conditions' were unprecedented and when what was known as the dole amounted I believe to $515,000,000. In the last three or four years they have paid off over $100,000,000 and in addition have laid up a rest of $225,000,000 to $250,000,000. The fund is now on a solvent basis.
When I asked the chief of the department at Whitehall what will happen when all these hundreds of thousands of men now engaged in munition work are laid off, perhaps because of sufficiency of munitions, he said: "Oh, we are now in a position to take care of that almost indefinitely." In the old land, therefore, they have fully demonstrated that their system is a sound one, and from my observation it is of tremendous benefit to the worker. To assure myself of its benefit to the worker I visited many plants and many employers and employees, but I shall tell of only three, widely different.
I went to a great steel plant employing 36,000 men. I talked to the foreman in front of the Bessemer furnace, where there was also a squad of four men. I asked him what he thought of unemployment insurance. He was a Scotsman. He replied, "Man, it is marvellous; it is wonderful. I have a wife and six children; I have not been out of work during the last three years and therefore have not required any unemployment benefit, but if I were out of work I would receive for myself $4.14 a week, for my wife S2.19, and for the children 49 cents each, plus 25 per cent." That would make for that man $11.95 a week, and he would receive it almost indefinitely; because for a man who has been on for that length of time the benefits continue for well on to a hundred weeks. In this country when a man is laid off he receives nothing; he either goes on charity or goes to the relief office to get something to exist on. It is a strange travesty that such a situation should exist in a land like ours, flowing as it is with milk and honey.
Then I went to a restaurant. In the British act they have not the restrictions on the number of employees that are imposed in the United States act, to which I shall refer later. The waiter at the restaurant told me he was married and had three children, and that if he were laid off he would receive within three days' time S9.75 a week. In London a man can live on $9.75 a week if he is not too extravagant. Then I went to a corner grocery, operated by a man and his wife and two employees. The man and his wife were
[Mr. MacNicol.!
working in the store; one employee was drawing a sick benefit of 17 shillings a week, together with medical attention and medicines, and the other young man, who was off because of unemployment, received $5.17 a week. Unemployment insurance in Great Britain is so all-embracing that over 18,000,000 out of the 20,000,000 employed are protected by the benefits of the unemployment insurance law. I often say to myself that when times are good in Canada again and we want more immigration-and we shall, because I am convinced we must have immigration to keep this country on an even keel-we shall have great difficulty in getting Britishers to come out They will say, "Why should we go out there? At home we have health insurance and unemployment insurance, whereas in Canada you have neither." The result will be that we shall have great difficulty in convincing immigrants qualified to render efficient service in Canada to leave the dear old land and come to this country-despite the fact that we have a land which does flow with milk and honey.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

If it does not take too
long to answer it.

Did the hon. member
visit any farms in Great Britain? Could he tell us about the activities on the farms?

I did not visit any farms, but I know that farm employees are now operating under the benefits of the unemployment. insurance scheme.
In Great Britain there is the widest possible extension of the benefits of unemployment insurance. As a matter of fact, I intended to refer to the classes receiving it when I discussed the United States system at a later point in my observations.
The German system, while a very good one, is not at all equal to that of Great Britain. But it does include three things, the first of which is accident insurance. If a worker is injured through an accident he will receive accident compensation. Their system includes invalidity insurance and unemployment insurance. The three are grouped together and, to that extent, in my judgment it is beneficial. The rates are however, much higher in Germany than in Great Britain, and the return is much lower. It is a federal-state system, and I assume they have not been able to adjust the operation as accurately and efficiently, on account of its being a federal-state system, as is the situation in the old land. The benefits in Germany do not range nearly as high. A married man with no

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. MacNicol.
dependents would receive from SI 50 to S4.92 a week. If he had dependents he would receive from S3.12 to S8.40 a week. The general application of the system in Germany is, in my opinion, not at all comparable with the application of the system in the old land.
Before I proceed to a discussion of unemployment insurance in the United States, it might be well to place before hon. members the scope of the British system. As I said a moment ago, in Great Britain the scope covers approximately 18,000,000 workers out of a possible 20,000,000. Contributions are at the rate of 20 eents a week by the employer, 20 cents by the employee and 20 cents by the state. The conditions stipulate that an employee must have made 30 contributions in a period of two years, and that fact is demonstrated by his presenting at the office an unemployment insurance card bearing 30 stamps. The waiting period is set at three days, and as benefits a man receives 17 shillings a week, a wife 9 shillings, and each child 3 shillings plus 25 per cent. The duration ordinarily runs from 26 to 52 weeks.
In cases where an employee has worked a considerable length of time without drawing anything from the unemployment insurance scheme, that period is considerably extended. In my judgment the system in operation in Great Britain is the best in the world.
Perhaps before proceeding to the situation in the United States, I should refer to the former Canadian legislation, which covered about 1,700,000 workers in Canada. Contributions were as follows: 25 cents from the employer, 25 cents from the employee and 10 cents plus costs from the state. In Great Britain the fund pays all costs. The legislation in Canada provided for 40 contributions in a period of two years. The waiting period was set at six days, and the benefits for a husband $6 a week, for a wife $2.70 and for a child 90 cents. The duration was set at from 78 to 100 days.
I now come to a discussion of what has been done in the United States in connection with unemployment insurance. For a long time an ardent and diligent study of the problem was made in that country. I have visited many of the separate states, and made a particular study in the state of Wisconsin where the scheme was first in operation. The states had some data to work on, compiled by some of their larger companies, which had in operation private unemployment insurance schemes. In this connection I would mention the General Electric Company, the American Radiator Company, Proctor and Gamble, and some others. In addition they had the benefit of the investigations made by many out-of-work benefit societies. Several
of the governors in eastern, central and western states, in their desire to bring about an unemployment insurance scheme, made a thorough survey in the respective sections.
The United States chamber of commerce made a most exhaustive survey which covered a period of about two years. All the information gathered was submitted to the government at Washington, at which time governmental officials began to realize what they were up against. They were faced with a problem similar to that in Canada, namely the sovereignty of the states. They realized the difficulty they would have in persuading each state of the union to adopt an unemployment insurance scheme.
The final contribution in each state amounts to three per cent of the wage-roll of companies employing eight or more employees. The amount has not, however, always been that much. It started at a lower figure. In one year it stood at 2-7 per cent. After the two-year intervening waiting period has expired the amount in all of the states will be three per cent. The act in the United States does not cover anything like the percentage covered in Great Britain. In the United States agricultural workers are not covered, whereas in Great Britain they are. Of those gainfully employed only 45-6 per cent would be receiving unemployment insurance in the country to the south of us.
Percentage of what?
The percentage of the number employed. For instance, there are 40,832,000 workers in factories, and in industrial pursuits, and there are 38,000,000 agricultural workers of one kind or another.
The British act is thirty years old.
Yes, I said it came into force in 1911. I will refer to that in a minute.
In the beginning a smaller number were included.

Under the legislation in the United States about 45-6 per cent of the workers would receive the benefits. I have no doubt, however, that as the United States gains experience in the operation of the legislation, it may reach the high point of operation which has been attained in Great Britain As a rule the people in our neighbouring country like to excel, and I have no doubt, when their act has been in operation as long as the British act, it will be a first-class piece of legislation, too.
As a matter of fact, in 1911, at the time of the commencement of the operation of the act in Great Britain, only 2,500,000 workers were
1118	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. MacNicol.
covered. After, however, a series of amendments through the years it has arrived at a stage wherein it covers 18,000,000 workers.
When the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) speaks, I should like him, if he has the information available, to tell the house if it is possible to adopt in Canada a measure anything like that adopted in the United States. Over there they have placed a tax on all companies employing eight or more men, although that regulation does not apply to all the states. I have not time to deal with the practice in all the separate states, but I know that in some there is reference to only four employees and, in others, to only five. Generally, however, I believe over half of the states make the provision for eight or more employees. In some states the employee makes a contribution, I believe of one per cent, but in the great majority of cases the contribution is made by the employer. I understand this contribution is three per cent of the wage-roll.
It is administered by the state.

Yes. As I understand it, the federal government-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-collect the three percent. They then say to the state, "We have prepared a sample unemployment insurance act; if your state adopts this act, or one similar to it to conform to your own conditions, we will return to you ninety per cent of the contribution." I believe that is the percentage.
Yes.

The federal government tell the state that they will pay the cost of administration. If a state does not accept that proposition, the money collected is used for public works or unemployment relief within the state. That might not be possible under our system of government. Every state in the American union has adopted an unemployment insurance act, and I believe they will all be in operation within another one or two years. Within two years at least every one of the forty-eight states and the District of Columbia will have systems of unemployment insurance in operation.
I do hope something can be done in this country. Industry is paying a heavy toll to-day. More factories are closing up than are opening. What can be done, I do not know, but the government should not delay. The need is greater than ever. The savings of the people have been exhausted. I know many of these people intimately, and I have been told their trials and troubles, their 
sorrows and joys. The stories are heartbreaking. Many of them have lost their little homes, and many others are in no state to combat present day conditions. We must be thankful that the depression has not lowered the moral standards of our people, but their physical standards have been decreased. Many men could not take the positions to-day that they could have taken a few years ago. In my judgment there are several reasons why we should have unemployment insurance.
The first is the fact that many men lose their employment because of age. Two weeks ago last Saturday when I was home a man came to see me who had worked eighteen years for a large company on Dufferin street and had finally been let out. That was a substantial length of time for a man to render service to a company. To have held his job that long he must have been an efficient workman. If he had not been honest and capable he would have been discharged long ago. After eighteen years this company said to him, "your services are no longer required." I saw him last Saturday and he told me that in an effort to save what he could, he had sacrificed his small home at such a reduction that all his life savings, barring a few hundred dollars, had disappeared. This man is about sixty years of age and I ask: What hope is there for him? I contend that there should be some arrangement, either governmental or otherwise, to take care of a man who had rendered eighteen years' efficient service.
We take care of our civic employees who subscribe to a fund. We take care of our civil servants. We have perhaps one of the best civil services in the world and they deserve all credit for their ability, but this government contributes toward their retirement. These people are taken care of, but not the poor chap who has no government or any other person to come to his defence when he loses his job. It does not seem right to me. Much of the unrest in Canada to-day is a result of the fact that no provision is made for these men. It might be said, "Why did not that man save something during his eighteen years of work?" I doubt if that man made more than $15 per week, and 1 defy anyone to save much on that salary when supporting a wife and family. He did save something, but when a man making $10,000 a year cannot save, we cannot expect the poor fellow getting $15 a week to do very much. I could relate other cases with which I am personally familiar, but I shall not at this time.

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Maclnnis
The next reason is invalidity. I shall review one or two cases in this connection, as my time will soon be up. I know one man who worked in front of a cupola. I have done it myself and I know something about the work. The other day we heard from a moulder from Vancouver who is also a lawyer. He delivered a fine speech in this house, and perhaps, if I were a lawyer, I could also deliver a good speech. But I come back to this poor fellow. He worked in front of that cupola for fourteen years, putting up with the heat in summer and the cold in winter. His health finally became undermined; he could not carry on with his work, and the company told him his services were no longer required. That is not fair treatment. If this government will introduce some legislation for a contributory scheme of unemployment insurance, one that will take care of the poor fellows who are now employed but who may soon be in the same boat as the chaps I have mentioned, they will be rendering a great service to this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to rise and say a few words in support of the motion introduced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). The subject matter of his resolution is one which the group to which I belong have had at heart for a long time. Before, however, I proceed with what I have to say, I should like to answer the question asked by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) who has just taken his seat. The hon. member said that almost everyone in the community is protected except the poor working man, that he did not have anyone to protect him or plead his case. He asked why that was so. He gave the answer himself. The reason he is not protected is that he has had no one to plead his case in the forums where such questions are discussed and decided. When he was speaking on the address the leader of the .opposition (Mr. Manion) made the statement that Canada was far behind all other British dominion's in the matter of social legislation. He asked why that should be. The reason for that is equally clear. Canada is behind the other dominions in the matter of labour organization, both industrial and political. It is the pressure by labour organizations on the industrial field and in parliament that gets results for the working classes.
I wish to commend the hon. member for Comox-Alberni for the brevity and conciseness of his motion. I do not think he has put in it a word that was not necessary or left
one out that was required. For the purposes of discussion his motion may be divided into four parts. First, he points out the urgent need in this country for unemployment insurance. Second, he contends that this need is so urgent that it should receive the immediate attention of the government. Third, he suggests that the plan of social insurance should be contributory in character and, fourth, that it should be national in scope.
I shall try to discuss these points in the order in which I have stated them. First, as to the pressing need for unemployment insurance; I think we are all agreed, and when I say there is a pressing need for unemployment insurance I have in mind that there is a need for a better method of distributing income to the worker, when, through no fault on his part, he is unemployed, than that which prevails to-day. One of the desirable features of an unemployment insurance plan is that those-who come under it, after complying with certain conditions known beforehand, will automatically participate in the benefits without having to go through the degrading process they must go through at present before obtaining unemployment relief. I think I am correct in saying that everyone in Canada who has given thought to this matter or who has given consideration to social conditions is in favour of a better method for the distribution of income. Of course I do not contend that unemployment insurance is a perfect method, but I do think it is a decided improvement over the system we follow at present.
The second point in the resolution is that the need for unemployment insurance is so urgent that it should be put into operation without delay. I believe there is very little difference of opinion on that point. We have had unemployment on a large scale for the past ten years, and there is no indication that we are nearing the end of our difficulties in that regard. Indeed, every indication is to the contrary, and I believe it is generally accepted that unemployment conditions of the past few years will be permanent as long as our present system of production and distribution continues. Such being the case, the government should act in this matter with the least possible delay. There has been, indeed, an insistent and widespread demand in Canada for a very long time for unemployment insurance. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) says for the last thirty years. I am not sure if it is that long, but it is at least twenty years. In looking over the records of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada recently, I found that in 1921 this organization went on
1120	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Maclnnis
record as being in favour of unemployment insurance. Whether or not there was an earlier discussion of the matter I do not know. The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada represents the largest number of organized workers in Canada, and I think every year since 1921, in their submissions to the federal cabinet, unemployment insurance has been advocated. The All-Canadian Congress of Labour, in their interviews with the government during the last few years, have also advocated unemployment insurance. The Federation of Catholic Workers and the Canadian Federation of Labour, for the last two years at least, have stressed the need for this kind of social insurance.
In 1919 a royal commission under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice L. G. Mathers was appointed to investigate industrial relations within the Dominion of Canada. After many hearings, and after visiting every industrial centre from Victoria to Sydney, the commissioners stated that fear of unemployment'was the chief cause of industrial unrest, and submitted a definite finding as part of their report. There are three short paragraphs in that report, which, I think, are worth reading to the house. The report can be found as an appendix to the report of the national industrial conference of 1919, and the sections to which I refer are on page 8:
34.	But supplying the unemployed man with suitable work for the present will not entirely solve the problem. Before the labourer can be made contented the haunting fear of unemployment must be removed from his mind.
35.	This is something which affects all wage-earners, but more especially the casual labourer. He can never be sure just when his employment will terminate and he will be left without the means of subsistence.
36.	Unemployment may arise from other [DOT]causes than the loss of his job. He may be
incapacitated by sickness, invalidity or old age. Very few labourers are able, out of their earnings, to make provision for these contingencies. We recommend to your government the question of making some provision by a system of state social insurance for those who through no fault of their own are unable to work, whether the inability arises from lack of opportunity, sickness, invalidity or old age. Such insurance would remove the spectre of fear which now haunts the wage earner, and make him a more contented and better citizen.
I submit that if the worker had been strongly represented in this parliament since 1919, unemployment insurance would have been on the statute books before now.
Might I ask the date of that report?

This was the Mathers commission, which sat in 1919.
I really do not think it necessary to elaborate on the need for unemployment in-

surance. I am convinced that there is so much unanimity on the subject that opposition to the principle is no longer an obstacle to the enactment of legislation. I am therefore in agreement with the mover of this motion, that the need is so urgent that it should receive the immediate attention of the government.
This brings me to the third point in the motion, that the insurance scheme or plan should be contributory in character. By that I understand the hon. member for Comox-Alberni to advocate a system of unemployment insurance under which the insured worker would make weekly or monthly contributions when employed. I am accepting that feature of the motion also. That is as far as I am called upon to go at this time. If we were discussing a bill instead of a resolution I might have something further to say on that point.
As far as I am able to learn, in all countries, with the possible exception of Russia, in which they have unemployment insurance it is on a contributory basis. The representatives of organized labour have gone on record as approving the contributory principle. If, as I said, we were discussing a bill, serious consideration would have to be given to workers in the low wage class, and exemptions might have to be made from the contributory principle. But I need not discuss that, because it is not before us. The fact, however, must be kept in mind that, with the very low wages prevailing in Canada at the present time, we might not be serving any useful purpose in taking money from people, who are not getting sufficient to maintain a decent standard of living or enough to keep them in normal health, in order to provide for a future contingency.
I think we should also try to get it clearly in our minds that insurance is not a solution for the problem of unemployment. It will not meet the needs of all the unemployed and much less will it prevent unemployment. We must face the fact that the kind of unemployment insurance we have in mind when discussing this resolution will not touch thousands of those who are unemployed to-day. There is, however, a turn-over in employment -if that is the correct term to use. That is, many workers are employed part of the time, and part of the time are out of work. Such workers would benefit under a plan such as we have in mind. How many workers would be covered by a scheme I do not know, possibly about a million and three quarters. On the other hand, thousands of those contributing would never draw financial benefits. That, however, is a condition inseparable from almost any kind of insurance.

Unemployment Insurance-
-Mr. Maclnnis
But as it is conceded that such a scheme would have a stabilizing effect on employment, benefits would accrue to all although it would be difficult to compute them in dollars and cents.
I agree with the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) that unemployment insurance means the sharing of the hazards of industrial employment; it is a realization of the fact that under our present economic arrangement a certain amount of unemployment is inevitable and that financial provision should be made to meet it.
In this connection I should like to give a very few statistics from the British Labour Gazette. This quotation appears in the January issue of the Canadian Congress Journal.
According to recent statistics published in the Labour Gazette, official organ of the British ministry of labour, 1,679,000 insured persons between the ages of sixteen and sixty-four out of a total number covered by the unemployment insurance plan of 12,250,000 were registered as unemployed at the employment exchanges in Great Britain on November 14, 1938.
The report says:
It is interesting to note that of this number 1.084,187, had been on the register less than three months, and approximately 825,000 persons, or 49-1 per cent of the total number of applicants, had been on the register for less than six weeks.
There were 165,690 persons, or 9*9 per cent of the total, who had been on the register f<pr more than three months but less than six months; 86,911 persons, or 5-2 per cent of the total, who had been on the register for more than six months but less than nine months; 64,636 persons, or 3-8 per cent of the total, who had been on the register for more than nine months but less than twelve months; leaving only 278,387 persons, or 16-6 per cent of the total who had been registered as unemployed continuously for more than a year.
I believe it is a tendency of our industrial set-up that those who work have more continuity of employment, while those who are out of work are out of work nearly all the time.
I must say again that I am not supporting or proposing unemployment insurance as a cure for unemployment. It has not accomplished that anywhere. But I know of no country that has put unemployment insurance on its statute books which has repealed that law. That is an indication that the law is meeting a social need and that the sooner we get it on the statute books of Canada, the better.
The fourth point in the motion is that unemployment insurance should be national in scope. I am also in full agreement with the mover of the motion in that regard. I believe that any attempt to legislate in this matter on a provincial basis would be 71492-71
fraught with considerable danger. It is not necessary at the moment to go into the many factors which would make it very difficult to administer a provincial scheme. There is also the fact that the majority of the provinces are not in a position financially to carry unemployment insurance; for one or two to embark on the scheme would only increase our difficulties, create more friction between the provinces and the dominion, and add to the factors which make for national disunity. I have the greatest regard for my own province of British Columbia, but I am a Canadian first and a British Columbian second. I am anxious in every way possible. to serve my people and add to th :r security and wellbeing, and I am satisfied I can do that to the best advantage by giving power to the federal authority to deal for the whole of Canada with those questions which, because of changed economic conditions, have become national in scope. I am thoroughly convinced that much of the talk we hear to-day about the sacredness of provincial rights and the determination in some quarters to maintain those rights at all costs has nothing more substantial behind it than the desire for power on the part of certain individuals whom accident or chance has thrown into positions of authority, and who, having become intoxicated with a little power, seek to hold on to it at no matter what cost to the whole of the country. I will go further and say that those leaders who are opposed to giving the federal authority the power to deal with matters of this kind are not expressing the desires of the people of their provinces. The people are looking for economic security and social well-being, and are not concerned with maintaining constitutional relations which were just and proper in their time but which to-day have become a fetter on social progress. Insistence on the maintenance of provincial rights to the point where that insistence retards national progress becomes, in my opinion, provincial stupidity.
Unemployment insurance is of the utmost importance to Canada to-day. Even though it will not meet the needs of many of the unemployed, it is no small thing to put thousands of workers now employed in a position where when they become unemployed they can maintain themselves and their families without having to submit to the degrading experience of those unfortunates who to-day must apply for unemployment relief. I believe that the federal government should go directly to the people of those provinces whose governments are retarding the enactment of this much-needed legislation and tell the people

1122	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Maclnnis
clearly and in language that cannot be misunderstood what they are anxious to do and what is keeping them from doing it.
The people of Canada are demanding unemployment insurance as they demanded old age pensions a little more than a decade ago. In that regard I should like to quote a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the session of 1926 when the old age pensions legislation was being debated. I am not sure whether this discussion was on the resolution or on the bill, but I rather think it was on the bill. The present leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), then a member of the house, was showing by the reading of letters that had passed between the dominion government and the provinces that the provincial governments were opposed to old age pensions. The Prime Minister said, as reported in Hansard of 1926, volume III, page 2487:
In reference to the answers from the nine provinces, which the hon. gentleman has just read, I might say that those very replies convinced the government of the futility of ever having an old age pension scheme enacted by correspondence with the provinces. We concluded that the best way would be to enact concrete legislation. We thought that was the only way to get anywhere.
I commend the Prime Minister for his determination on that occasion, and I think that if he were to show the same kind of determination now, ways and means could be found to put unemployment insurance on the statute books in spite of the provinces, and that the people of the provinces would compel their governments to take advantage of it in the same way as they compelled them to take advantage of the benefits of the Old Age Pensions Act. For the past eight years the international labour office at Geneva has issued a year book in which is reviewed, among other things concerning labour, the progress and extension of social insurance all over the world. At the conclusion of the review in the 1938 year book they refer to social insurance. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) mentioned that in the old country unemployment insurance now covers agricultural as well as industrial workers, and in the year book this statement appears with reference to agricultural workers:
Social insurance has another very important task to perform, namely, the extension of its protection to rural as well as to urban workers. This extension, which necessitates the adaptation of methods to rural conditions, is perfectly feasible, as is proved by the experience of many countries which have developed agricultural insurance schemes resolutely and methodically.

Agriculture is becoming more and more industrialized, and this process calls for new

forms of social protection. A large field of activity is being thrown open to social insurance in the agricultural countries, and the considerable experience already gained in this field should permit them to adapt themselves rapidly to the requirements of their task.
Social insurance of independent -workers.- Another important aspect of the recent development of social insurance is its extension to independent workers. In many countries craftsmen, traders, small farmers, professional workers and other independent workers with limited incomes are calling for measures to give them security in their old gae. Though formerly violently opposed to every kind of collective protection, they have come to realize the material and moral value of insurance and desire to benefit from it in their turn.
* * #
Social insurance can neither heal nor prevent all ills. Its resources and practical possibilities, though considerable, are limited, and its action must be kept within measured hounds. Whenever the necessity of such action is recognized, however, it should be effective and adequate. The effort of organization and social solidarity represented by social insurance needs to he continued and, in many cases, intensified. A lasting civilization is unthinkable except on the basis of a new economic and social order in which workers will enjoy, not only a higher standard of living, but also the absolute guarantee of complete economic security.
I do not suggest that unemployment insurance on the scale on which it could be adopted in this country at the moment could give that adequate and complete guarantee, but I do insist that it is a step towards that desirable end. To what I have just read I should like to add this as my own considered opinion. I believe it is now generally admitted that further progress in the material sphere cannot be achieved without a system of social security that makes provision for a more equitable distribution of the national income than now prevails and that will protect workers and their families from many of the vicissitudes of life.
Any program of economic recovery and prosperity runs the risk of failure if it does not include a soundly conceived social plan. The world's productive capacity in labour and material has for the past hundred and fifty years been kept busy building a capital structure, that is, producing equipment for the production of wealth. In the opinion of many that work is now finished. If, then, we are to keep busy the machines which were built with much labour and privation we must find ways of financing consumption. I must have borrowed that phrase unconsciously from the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), but in this case it is a good phrase. Social insurance is one of the ways in which this can be, at least partly, done. I am not arguing that it is the best way, but it is the way most universally accepted.

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Reid
We cannot move much faster than we have public opinion with us, without some danger to the stability of the social structure. But we cannot stand still. Move we must or perish. The need for social insurance is being universally recognized. The principle	of
social protection is winning the day against the anarchy of individualism. The work of social organization, however, is only beginning; it must be vigorously pushed forward; for in our changing world that is the price of lasting progress. The premium paid for social insurance is small compared with the risks that confront humanity if it refuses or is unable to master the forces of production at its disposal and distribute the product fairly.
In concluding these few remarks, I think we should take a vote on this question and make it clear beyond the possibility of doubt that this house stands solidly behind the government in support of a plan of unemployment insurance national in scope. The unanimous endorsation by this house of the principle expressed in this resolution would do much to strengthen the hands and, I hope, the determination of the government to press forward with unemployment insurance with all speed. At the very root of the friction and bickerings which menace the unity and progress of our country lies the fear engendered by poverty and insecurity When the people of this dominion are linked together, not by a legal constitution but by common economic and social ties, when they begin to look to the federal government as the seat of authority and the centre from which they can expect guidance in solving those problems which face all the people, they will quickly begin to acquire that attitude and outlook so essential to national unity and nationhood.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Reid
a mere statistical view of our present economic situation. After all, statistics do not always reveal the actual situation.
Great Britain was the first nation to take a long term realistic view of her internal affairs and so saved that country from internal disorders if not from actual revolution itself. Recognizing that insecurity is inherent in the modern industrial business structure, Great Britain provided economic security for her people through an elaborate social system. As a result Great Britain spent for social insurance, including payments to the unemployed, the sick, the injured, the aged and the widows and children, a total of SI,369,000,000 in 1933. By this means Great Britain has preserved and is preserving the British democratic form of government, thereby giving renewed faith and inspiration to the British people in their own system of democratic government, something which I fear we might be in some danger of losing in Canada to-day.
Unfortunately the blind greed and stupidity of our business leaders and some of their political allies fail to recognize the growing storm of discontent gradually creeping over Canada to-day.
Relief, it is true, is being provided on a scale hitherto unknown in this country, but in the giving of relief even under the most favourable conditions and even though essentials of life are provided it should not be forgotten that relief violates man's most valued possession-his self-esteem.
The question of social security to my mind does not and should rest not entirely on economic grounds but on humanitarian grounds as well. What great value should be attached to any economic system if it cannot adequately meet the needs of all her people.
The system adopted by that great and wise nation Great Britain, one of progressive taxation and an adequate system of social security, is one of real merit and one well worth while considering and adopting. Our system, although somewhat progressive, has brought about no re-apportionment of our wealth; in fact, it has put and is to-day putting more wealth in the hands of the wealthy and making the poor even poorer.
The insecurity of our people to-day in the face of the hazards of modem life, with unemployment the chief hazard, menaces more than mere national prosperity. It endangers the very existence of our social order.
In closing, I would express my belief that if a plan such as I have outlined were put into effect, not only would it provide for greater employment of our young people, by removing persons of sixty and sixty-five from the labour market, but it would help to give 
a greater sense of security to our people and remove from our midst many of the disquieting fears which now confront us.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not take very much of the time of the house on this question. I rise merely to put myself in the position of supporting the resolution. The whole matter has been very thoroughly discussed here this afternoon by various speakers. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), who moved the resolution, and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who seconded it, dealt with it in detail. Others have also discussed the whole subject very fully. The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Reid) covered a little wider ground, by taking in old age pensions and social security in general; but whatever he does, the hon. gentleman has two qualifications which I rather like; one is industry and the other is the burr in his voice. One does not need to hear the skirl of the bagpipes when the hon. gentleman is speaking, because one knows at once whence he came and the kind of food on which he was brought up- porridge, mostly, I mean.
As the resolution is brief and covers the ground very fully, and since a good many other matters have been touched upon by various speakers in the course of the debate, I will take the liberty of reading it:
That in the opinion of this house, a national system of contributory unemployment insurance for Canada is a pressing need at the present time and should receive immediate attention.
I think it deserves the support of us all; and to show that our party is in good faith in supporting it I can adduce two very good proofs. One is the act which we put in force when this party was in power, in 1935, although the act was later pronounced ultra vires; the other is the resolution of the National Conservative convention held last July; it is brief, so I will read it:
To encourage and support throughout Canada a plan of national unemployment and retirement insurance.
That is a plank of our party's platform. The legislation we put into effect, and which was assented to on June 28, 1935, was, to quote the title:
An act to establish an employment and social insurance commission, to provide for a national employment service, for insurance against unemployment, for aid to unemployed persons, and for other forms of social insurance and security, and for purposes related thereto.
It is chapter 38 of the statutes of Canada, 1935, 25-26 George V. That legislation covered other ground than unemployment insurance.

Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Manion
For example, section 7 points out that the commission which was to be appointed shall, in addition to its powers and duties as otherwise provided by this act-

as soon as practicable after appointment, undertake investigations for the purpose of making proposals to the governor general in council for-
-various other matters, such as:
-providing unemployment insurance for the employments excepted from the operation of part III of the act.
And so on. On the next page provision is included for training of the unemployed- something which has been taken up by this government to a certain extent in recent times. In part II an employment service was proposed. I will read section 10:
The commission shall organize an employment service for the Dominion of Canada, in manner hereinafter provided, and shall be responsible for the constitution and management of such employment service and the direction, maintenance and control of all employment offices established as hereinafter provided.
That is very much what was proposed, I believe, by the Purvis commission, although not carried out by the government.
This resolution is in accord with the act as we passed it, because it makes insurance contributory. Section 17 states:
(1) The funds required for providing unemployment benefit and for making any other payments which under this act are to be made out of the unemployment insurance fund, established under this part of this act, shall be derived partly from moneys provided by parliament, partly from contributions by employed persons and partly from contributions by the employers of those persons, which contributions shall be paid by means of revenue stamps as hereinafter provided, or otherwise as may be prescribed by the commission.
That is all I shall quote from the act, which is a very complete one. Quite frankly, at the time of its passing I was not as familiar with it as I might have been. It was handled through the Department of Labour, then under Hon. W. A. Gordon, and at that time I was minister of railways. Nevertheless I well remember long discussions in council, prolonged disputes about certain industries which insisted upon being exempted from the provisions of the act. At the same time the whole act is so complete that when this government finally decides to bring into effect legislation along the lines of the resolution, it might well be based upon the act of 1935, with, possibly, modifications to meet some changed conditions.
I do believe that had the act as passed been put into effect, leaving a private individual to bring it before the courts, it would still 71492-72
be in force. If, instead of being submitted to the courts for decision, that act had been placed in operation, it might still be operating to-day. When something is a jait accompli, it is rare that action is taken against it unless it is distinctly injurious, and this is not an injurious measure. I believe unemployment insurance will have to be brought into operation in the near future, whether this government institutes it or whether the successor to this government takes the initiative. I say that because to my mind legislation such as is in force in so many other countries-England, Australia, New Zealand, and the United States more recently, to mention a few-is recognized everywhere as necessary under modern conditions of employment or unemployment as you will, and it must be so recognized in Canada also.
I believe I have made the criticism in this house, as I have done elsewhere, that the trouble with the Canadian people is that we are less advanced than the people of almost any of the modern countries. The most advanced country, as was said by the Iron, member who has just taken his seat, is probably Great Britain. I myself have made that statement on many platforms, and I believe that if we were more ready to copy Great Britain in her advanced legislation, as so often we are prepared to copy her in other matters, we should be showing a progressive spirit and putting into effect ideas appropriate to this great country.
We must do whatever we can to bring about security for our people. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) the other day, in offering some criticism of myself, said that I do not propose much that is constructive. On one occasion before the Canadian club in Ottawa-it was a year ago last month-when his leader the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was present, and when the minister himself, I believe, was in attendance, I did suggest unemployment insurance. That was one of the constructive ideas I put forward at that time, and I offered many other suggestions of a progressive sort on that occasion-so many, in fact, that the present leader of the government came up to me and remarked that I had made the best Liberal speech he had heard. Well, theoretically it was a Liberal speech. The trouble is that this Liberal government is progressive only in theory. Unfortunately it does not go ahead in practice and do what it promises in theory.
The point I wish to make now is that in this democratic British country we must cure the conditions from which we are suffering to-day. If what I have described as the great defect of democracy, unemployment, is

1130	COMMONS
Unemployment Insurance-Mr. Manion
not remedied, then I am afraid that the system under which we live will not last very long. For saying that on a number of occasions in speeches that were more or less political, though I have said the same thing in other speeches, before Canadian clubs and elsewhere, I have been accused of being too radical. I repeat, however, that if we do not bring into effect measures which will cure unemployment, measures which will take care of those who are out of work through no fault of their own, I sincerely believe that this democratic system will not continue. In a country such as this, rich in resources, with a sparse population and a huge area, people will not continue indefinitely to put up with conditions such as those under which they live in Canada to-day, with 800,000 people on relief and practically half a million unemployed. And, personally I do not think that they should.
If the British democratic system, not only in Canada, but in the United States, in Great Britain and in France cannot solve the problems that face these countries to-day, then I do not think it is worth saving. I do not believe in the socialism suggested by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I believe in the present capitalist system properly improved to meet the difficulties that exist under it. As I say, I do not believe in socialism. Rather, I want to see the present economic system, the present British democratic system with its parliamentary and other liberties maintained. But I do not think that this system can be maintained unless we cure the evils which exist under it. To me that is a particularly strong argument for something being done about the condition which we are now discussing.
I know that the attitude the government takes is that the trouble lies with the British North America Act; the trouble is in getting that act changed. Well, I do not think that is necessary. Action could be taken by cooperation with the provinces. Mr. Duplessis, the Premier of Quebec, is one of those who have been quoted as opposing any change in the British North America Act, as is his right, but even he, in the last paragraph of his letter dated December 30, 1937, makes a suggestion to the Prime Minister. In the earlier paragraphs of the letter he opposes any change in the act, but in the concluding paragraph he states:
In conclusion, again I state that the province of . Quebec is willing to cooperate heartily in the establishment of a sound and fair system of unemployment insurance, which could be established on a national scope, without infringing upon the rights and autonomy . of the provinces.
fMr. Manion.}
I assume the Minister of Labour will deal with that. I admit that it might not be as satisfactory as a national system which could be put into effect if a change were made in the British North America Act; but under the circumstances, with certain provinces refusing to consent to any change in the act, I see no reason why unemployment insurance could not be put into effect along the lines suggested by Mr. Duplessis.

Is the hon. gentleman aware that in August, 1934, I believe, the government of which he was a member did invite the provinces to attend a conference to consider, among other things, the transfer of jurisdiction over unemployment insurance to the dominion parliament? That conference was never held. The government of which he was a member appropriated in a sense the authority over unemployment insurance. In other words, there was an assertion on the part of the government that the power to enact an unemployment insurance scheme lay with the dominion parliament, and it was against that view that the privy council ultimately gave its decision.

I have no quarrel with that. I do not remember the incident, but the hon. gentleman is Minister of Labour and I was minister of railways at the time, so that I am not as familiar with that aspect as he might be. But I do not see that his statement changes the facts. Men like Mr. Bennett, who was a constitutional lawyer, Mr. Guthrie, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart), the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), who have all studied the problem in its constitutional aspects, apparently came to the conclusion-a conclusion to which naturally I could take no exception, not being a lawyer-that it was within our jurisdiction; and we thought it was; for we put into effect the legislation from which I have quoted. Incidentally, two judges, Chief Justice Duff and Mr. Justice Davis, both gave judgment in favour of it. They are two of the outstanding judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. Be that as it may, it was declared ultra vires by the supreme court, and that decision was upheld by the privy council. That being so, without quarrelling about the question of jurisdiction, I say, let us in fairness and honesty, instead of merely expressing so many theoretical and pious platitudes, put the legislation into effect as suggested by Mr. Duplessis. Let us put it into effect, leaving the right to the provinces to join and participate in its benefits. I venture to say that if that were done, all the provinces would in the near future join and cooperate, for the
